prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I still place the unfolded protein response among the strongest basic-science discoveries on the list, but after the first round I no longer think it should displace GLP-1 this year. The reason is the one my colleagues pressed on me: the GLP-1 line runs from proglucagon processing and human incretin physiology through the active truncated peptide to drugs with large, independently confirmed effects on diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes, while the UPR's route to patients remains indirect. Holst and Drucker are the secure core, and Mojsov's identification of the active peptide gives a discovery-centred third name. A single three-person prize also fits the limit exactly, so a second part is not possible without dropping a GLP-1 name, and I do not think the UPR case justifies that. My configuration is unchanged from round 1 in names and ballot, and I have adopted a slightly tighter citation.
statement.case_against: The third slot is still a judgement and not a settled fact. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested against Habener and colleagues, who are not credited, and I cannot verify that dispute from the supplied text. Leaving out Knudsen leaves out the person behind liraglutide and semaglutide, so a physiology-centred prize can be criticised as honouring the discovery and not the drug. All six round-1 files now converge on the same trio, and I am wary of reading that as evidence of correct attribution, since five of us were moved there partly by each other's reasoning and none of us has new primary-literature evidence. Finally, a GLP-1 prize uses every available name and defers B032, whose Walter and Mori pairing is the cleaner allocation and arguably as overdue.

responses.point: The chair moved from Knudsen to Mojsov for the third slot, wants the omission of Knudsen noted openly, and asks whether Mojsov's priority is secure enough to carry a laureate place.
responses.response: I agree with your move and with the request not to treat the omission as costless. On your question, I cannot call Mojsov's priority secure from the supplied text, but I also do not think the dispute removes her. The disagreement with Habener concerns who first identified and characterised the truncated insulinotropic form, and her contribution to its identification and synthesis is part of the discovery chain whichever way that dispute is settled. What would change my mind is primary-literature evidence that the active-form identification was fully established by an uncredited group before her work. Absent that, I would keep her. If the committee did flip to Knudsen, the citation would have to be rewritten around therapies, and then it must explain why Mojsov is left out, which is the harder explanation to give.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps B043 with Mojsov, states that he is relying on recollection of the priority record, and would revisit only if Mojsov's priority could not be defended, in which case Knudsen is the natural third name.
responses.response: That conditional is the right one, and I share it. Because neither of us has verified the priority record, I think the honest position is that the evidence is balanced and that the choice is between two defensible framings: discovery of the biology or translation to the drug. I would not let the lack of verification drive us to Knudsen by default, because that changes the character of the prize without new evidence. I also take your earlier point that a messy attribution does not lower the merit of the discovery. That is why I keep GLP-1 first even though its credit is less tidy than B032's.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that an unresolved priority dispute is a reason to scrutinise the primary literature and not to default to the cleanest alternative, and wants the citation to say plainly that it recognises translation if Knudsen is included.
responses.response: I agree that an open priority question should be examined and not resolved by retreating to B032, and my own move away from ranking the UPR first reflects that. I would add that this applies in both directions: an unresolved dispute is no reason to prefer the cleaner pairing, and it is no reason to presume Mojsov's claim is the weaker one. On the citation, I think the same principle applies to our configuration. Since Knudsen is omitted, the wording should tie the therapies to the discovery of the physiology and the active peptide, so that nobody reads the prize as a verdict on the drug programmes.

responses.point: El Manira says the clean allocation is an advantage B043 lacks, but asks for concrete disease-level evidence supporting UPR modulation before moving B032 above B043, and treats B032 only as a second alternative.
responses.response: That is a fair test and I cannot meet it from what we have. The UPR has well-documented links to proteostasis, diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer, but I cannot point to a modulating therapy with outcome-trial evidence comparable to the incretin drugs. The nearest examples, such as integrated stress response modulators, are early. So I accept that on consequence for human disease B043 is ahead, and I have changed my preferred configuration from my opening ballot accordingly. I would still hold B032 as the first alternative and the leading candidate for a later year, with the caveat from Perlmann and the chair that the PERK, ATF6 and integrated stress response arms, and the work of Ron and Kaufman, make its pairing less clean than it appears.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps B019 and B013 as alternatives, stresses demonstrated patient benefit, and asks which of CAR-T or cGAS-STING should be held for a later year given attribution and maturity.
responses.response: Applying your own criterion, I would hold CAR-T ahead of cGAS-STING. CAR-T has demonstrated patient benefit in refractory haematological cancers, while cGAS-STING is still early in therapeutic translation, although the mechanism is well established. CAR-T's weakness is attribution, since Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept sits outside the credited names, and I would want that resolved before treating it as a prize candidate. I therefore list B019 as my second alternative, and I would not move B013 up until it has clinical validation.

uncertainties: Mojsov's priority for the active peptide against Habener and colleagues cannot be settled from the supplied text, and nothing in round 1 added primary evidence either way.
Whether a physiology-centred prize without Knudsen is the better framing than a therapy-centred one, which is a value judgement about how far industrial analogue design counts as discovery.

Whether B032 should wait or whether deferring it risks leaving an overdue two-person discovery unrecognised; the PERK, ATF6, integrated stress response and Ron and Kaufman contributions also leave its attribution less clean than it looks.
Whether CAR-T can be allocated fairly without Eshhar.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates. I have co-authored with Linnarsson, Frisén and Burge's group, and none of them is credited on a shortlisted ballot. My work on RNA processing makes me familiar with the SMN2 splicing candidate (B029), which I do not propose. No recusal is needed, and nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
